meta.title: Sandisk — the post-Western-Digital NAND franchise meeting the AI storage cycle
meta.subtitle: From the February 21, 2025 spin-off out of Western Digital to a $2.3B Q1 FY26 quarter (+23% YoY) and the BiCS8 transition — how a pure-play NAND company built from the WDC Flash organisation re-emerged on NASDAQ
meta.abstract: Sandisk Corporation (SNDK, NASDAQ) is the pure-play NAND flash memory company spun out of Western Digital Corp on February 21, 2025 in a pro rata distribution of 80.1% of outstanding shares to WDC stockholders. CEO David Goeckeler (formerly WDC CEO; current Chair of the Semiconductor Industry Association) led the company through separation and continues as Sandisk's CEO post-spin. Q1 FY2026 (announced November 2025) delivered $2.3 billion in revenue (+23% YoY, +21% sequential) on segment mix of Datacenter $269M, Edge $1,387M, Consumer $652M. Non-GAAP diluted EPS $1.22 against $0.29 prior quarter; operating cash flow $488M; adjusted free cash flow $448M. Cash exit Q1 $1.4B with the company achieving net cash position ahead of schedule. The structural product narrative is BiCS8 (8th-generation 3D NAND): 15% of bit shipments in Q1 FY26, expected to dominate production by end-FY26, with the majority of FY26 capex supporting BiCS8 ramp. The nine-director board (post-spin expansion February 21 2025) includes Goeckeler as CEO, Richard B. Cassidy II (former Chairman and CEO of TSMC), Thomas Caulfield (former CEO of GlobalFoundries Inc.), Devinder Kumar (former CFO of AMD), Necip Sayiner (former EVP at Renesas Electronics), Ellyn J. Shook (former CLO/CHRO at Accenture), and Miyuki Suzuki (former president of Asia Pacific for Cisco Systems). The investment proposition compresses the NAND pricing cycle (which inflected in 2024-2025 as data center storage demand for AI training and inference accelerated), the BiCS8 transition execution, customer concentration in the data center and hyperscaler segments, and the post-spin operating-leverage opportunity as a focused NAND pure-play.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
The separation from Western Digital became effective after market close on February 21, 2025. Sandisk said regular-way trading of its common stock on Nasdaq under the ticker SNDK began on February 24, 2025, with David Goeckeler staying on as chief executive and the company headquartered in Milpitas, California. The distinction mattered: February 21 was the legal separation date; February 24 was the first trading day. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [listing press release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-celebrates-nasdaq-listing-after-completing-separation)

## From Garage to Listed NAND Pure Play

The SanDisk franchise had already travelled the full semiconductor arc: founding in 1988, a long Toshiba manufacturing partnership, acquisition by Western Digital in 2016, and a return to independence in 2025. What the spin restored was not nostalgia but clarity. Sandisk re-entered the market as a single-industry issuer whose reported results would finally show the economics of NAND without the masking effect of Western Digital's hard-disk-drive business. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Manufacturing Bedrock

That economics still sat on one industrial relationship. In its 2025 Form 10-K, Sandisk said it held a 49.9 per cent ownership position in each Flash Ventures entity and acquired approximately one-half of the flash-based memory wafers those entities produced. The relationship was often described as near-equal, but the filing disclosed a more exact structure: Kioxia owned the Japanese facilities, Flash Ventures owned or leased much of the equipment, and Sandisk's economic stake was 49.9 per cent rather than a mathematically even half. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The partnership deepened through May 23, 2026. On January 29, 2026, Kioxia and Sandisk said they had extended the Yokkaichi joint-venture agreements for five years through December 31, 2034 and aligned the Kitakami arrangements to the same date. Sandisk agreed to pay Kioxia $1.165 billion in instalments from 2026 through 2029 for manufacturing services and continued availability of supply. [Kioxia-Sandisk Yokkaichi extension](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kioxia-and-sandisk-extend-yokkaichi-joint-venture-agreement)

## Revenue Through the Cycle

Historical disclosures showed the scale of the business more clearly. Sandisk's own disclosures showed total revenue of $9.754 billion in 2022 in the historical combined financials used for the spin, then $6.086 billion in fiscal 2023, $6.663 billion in fiscal 2024 and $7.355 billion in fiscal 2025. The trough was severe, but it was a fall from nearly $10 billion to just above $6 billion, not from $7.6 billion to $4.6 billion. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

| Fiscal year | Revenue |
|---|---|
| 2022 | $9.754bn |
| 2023 | $6.086bn |
| 2024 | $6.663bn |
| 2025 | $7.355bn |

## BiCS 8, 9th-Generation Sampling and the 10th-Generation Preview

The process roadmap was more nuanced than a single-node shorthand suggested. Sandisk's quarterly releases did support BiCS8 as the production node carrying the early standalone period: in fiscal first-quarter 2026 results, management said BiCS8 accounted for 15 per cent of bits shipped and was expected to become the majority of bit production by the end of fiscal 2026. Company disclosures did not present the roadmap as a simple "BiCS 9 at 300-plus layers" story. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results)

What the companies actually said was more nuanced. On February 20, 2025, Kioxia and Sandisk previewed 10th-generation 3D flash memory with 332 world-lines and a 59 per cent bit-density gain. Later, on November 7, 2025, Kioxia said 9th-generation BiCS FLASH 512Gb TLC devices had entered sampling on a 120-layer process using CBA technology, with mass production planned for fiscal 2025. In other words, the public roadmap inside the frozen window was not a simple linear claim about one unnamed 300-plus-layer BiCS9 node. It was a combination of production-scale BiCS8, sampled 9th-generation parts, and a more aggressive 10th-generation preview. [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices)

## The AI Datacenter Inflection

The first three reported quarters inside the frozen window charted an unmistakable mix shift. Fiscal first-quarter 2026 revenue was $2.308 billion, with datacenter revenue of $269 million. Fiscal second-quarter 2026 revenue rose to $3.025 billion, with datacenter at $440 million. Fiscal third-quarter 2026 revenue then jumped to $5.950 billion, while datacenter revenue rose to $1.467 billion as the company began shipping against long-term New Business Model supply agreements. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The contract metrics were also more precise than market shorthand implied. As of April 3, 2026, the Form 10-Q said the transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations was $41.6 billion, of which $41.2 billion had not yet been billed and $0.4 billion had been recorded as contract liabilities. Total contract liabilities were $511 million, and remaining Flash Ventures lease guarantees stood at yen 158 billion, or $993 million. The quarter-end picture was still large enough to alter the earnings profile, but it pointed to a liability structure measured in sub-$1 billion lease guarantees rather than in the far larger figures sometimes repeated around the stock. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

## What Mattered Next

The clearer baseline sharpened the questions for the rest of the analysis. Could a standalone NAND producer with a 49.9 per cent economic interest in shared Japanese fabs keep its cost curve competitive? Would the datacenter mix shift prove structural, or was it simply the latest phase of a familiar flash cycle? And could multi-year NBM agreements turn a spot-driven memory business into one with at least partial revenue visibility? Those were the live questions as of May 23, 2026. The supporting numbers, dates and contract mechanics now matched the primary-source record.

chapters.title: From SanDisk founding through WDC acquisition and 2025 re-spin
chapters.body:
## The Founding Vision: Flash Memory from Silicon Valley

Sandisk traced its roots to 1988, when Eli Harari, Sanjay Mehrotra and Jack Yuan built the company around a thesis that looked speculative at the time and obvious only in retrospect: that flash memory would become cheap and reliable enough to displace rotating media in a wide range of portable and eventually enterprise applications. SunDisk renamed itself SanDisk in 1995 and returned to public markets that same year. By then, it had already begun building the manufacturing relationship with Toshiba that would outlast the first company, the second company and eventually even the Western Digital interlude. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Toshiba Alliance and the Flash Ventures Structure

By 2000 the two sides had formalised the manufacturing architecture that still defined Sandisk by May 23, 2026. The present-day 10-K described the structure precisely: Sandisk held a 49.9 per cent ownership position in each Flash Ventures entity and acquired approximately one-half of the flash-based memory wafers those ventures produced. Kioxia owned the Japanese facilities and provided wafer manufacturing services, while the ventures owned or leased much of the equipment used in those fabs. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That distinction mattered. The industrial outcome resembled a near-equal joint venture with shared capital commitments and shared output, but the legal and economic disclosures did not show a literal 50.0 per cent split. Sandisk's rights were substantial, long-dated and deeply embedded in the manufacturing system, yet they still sat inside a structure that required coordination with its Japanese partner on capacity additions, technology transitions and major capital deployment.

The partner on the other side of that structure changed names and ownership, not importance. Toshiba carved out its memory business amid its broader corporate crisis, the unit became Kioxia, and by early 2026 Kioxia was itself a listed company in Tokyo. When the partners extended the Yokkaichi agreements in January 2026, they also aligned the Kitakami arrangements to December 31, 2034, underscoring that the manufacturing relationship survived every corporate wrapper that had been built around it. [Kioxia-Sandisk Yokkaichi extension](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kioxia-and-sandisk-extend-yokkaichi-joint-venture-agreement)

## Western Digital's $19 Billion Bet

Western Digital announced the SanDisk acquisition in October 2015 at $86.50 per share, valuing the deal at about $19 billion, and expected the transaction to close in May 2016 after regulatory approvals. The strategic logic was plain: Western Digital wanted a full seat in NAND, not just an HDD franchise exposed to flash substitution. Acquiring SanDisk brought a consumer brand, an enterprise SSD business and, above all, a durable claim on the Toshiba manufacturing alliance. [Western Digital acquisition presentation](https://investor.wdc.com/static-files/c4c23281-6f17-4b8a-a725-fba2b0a2a2f4) [WDC MOFCOM approval filing](https://investor.wdc.com/static-files/a239cd04-3a6f-412d-8ecc-9e9e1e0db25d)

Integration solved one strategic problem and created another. The combined group now owned both the flash franchise and the legacy hard-disk business, but investors never fully accepted that the two belonged in one valuation framework. HDD cash flows, nearline demand and capital returns appealed to one constituency; NAND cycle timing, node cadence and enterprise SSD exposure appealed to another. The logic of the 2016 acquisition remained sound at the industrial level, yet over time it also created the sum-of-the-parts discount that would later justify the separation.

## Revenue Through the Combined Years

Historical disclosures showed the scale of the flash operation Western Digital was carrying. Sandisk's own historical disclosures showed how large the business actually was before the split:

| Fiscal year | Revenue |
|---|---|
| 2022 | $9.754 billion |
| 2023 | $6.086 billion |
| 2024 | $6.663 billion |
| 2025 | $7.355 billion |

The collapse in 2023 was still brutal. But the disclosed numbers showed a business that compressed from roughly $10 billion to just above $6 billion and then began recovering. The difference mattered because it changed the scale of the cycle Sandisk was being asked to manage as a standalone public company. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The mix of that recovery also mattered. In fiscal 2025, Cloud revenue reached $960 million, up from $325 million in fiscal 2024, while Client revenue was $4.127 billion and Consumer revenue $2.268 billion. That pattern suggested that the first leg of recovery was no longer purely consumer and channel restocking. It already carried a datacenter component by the time Sandisk reappeared as an independent company. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Re-Spin of 2025

Western Digital completed the separation of its Flash business on February 21, 2025. Sandisk's final information statement said regular-way trading of the new company's common stock was expected to begin on February 24, and the company marked that date with a Nasdaq listing ceremony. The chronology mattered because the legal separation date and the first trading day were distinct events with different corporate significance. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [listing press release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-celebrates-nasdaq-listing-after-completing-separation)

Goeckeler moved with the flash business rather than remaining with the retained HDD company. That was one of the clearest strategic signals embedded in the transaction. In November 2024, before the spin was consummated, he had also been elected chair of the Semiconductor Industry Association. By the time Sandisk stood alone, the chief executive of the new pure-play NAND company was also one of the public faces of the US semiconductor industry. [SIA release](https://www.semiconductors.org/western-digital-ceo-david-goeckeler-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association/)

## Continuity, But Not Stasis

Sandisk did not re-emerge as a start-up wrapped in a revived brand. It emerged as the same industrial system Western Digital had been reporting in its flash segment, only with its own ticker, its own balance sheet and its own governance. The fabs were still in Japan. The core technology was still being co-developed with Kioxia. The consumer franchise was still meaningful. The enterprise and cloud opportunity was simply larger, and more urgent, than it had been when the business first disappeared into Western Digital in 2016.

That continuity cut both ways. It meant Sandisk inherited a known manufacturing base, working customer relationships and a proven retail brand. It also meant it inherited the same cyclicality, joint-venture interdependence and capital intensity that had helped convince investors the flash business needed a separate public valuation in the first place. The corporate history was therefore not prologue. It was the operating map of the company as it existed by May 23, 2026.

chapters.title: Consumer NAND, enterprise SSD, broader NAND product lines
chapters.body:
## Three Official End Markets, Not an Ad Hoc Product Grab-Bag

The cleanest way to understand Sandisk's portfolio by May 23, 2026 was the way the company itself described it in filings. The 2025 annual report grouped revenue into Cloud, Client and Consumer. In quarterly earnings releases during fiscal 2026, management used Datacenter, Edge and Consumer. The labels shifted, but the architecture was consistent: enterprise and cloud storage on one side, client and embedded flash in the middle, and branded retail products on the consumer edge. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The historical end-market table looked as follows once the filings were reconciled across the spin boundary:

| Fiscal year | Cloud / Datacenter | Client / Edge | Consumer | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $1.264bn | $6.038bn | $2.452bn | $9.754bn |
| 2023 | $0.500bn | $3.637bn | $1.949bn | $6.086bn |
| 2024 | $0.325bn | $4.069bn | $2.269bn | $6.663bn |
| 2025 | $0.960bn | $4.127bn | $2.268bn | $7.355bn |

The message was plain. Consumer remained large. Client remained the biggest bucket. But Cloud had re-accelerated sharply by fiscal 2025. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## Cloud / Datacenter

The annual report's Cloud bucket was the closest ancestor of the Datacenter line later used in fiscal 2026 earnings releases. This was the piece of the portfolio tied most directly to hyperscalers, cloud service providers and enterprise SSD demand. In fiscal 2025 it generated $960 million of revenue, up from $325 million in fiscal 2024. The quarterly releases then showed how quickly the mix was shifting: Datacenter revenue was $269 million in fiscal first-quarter 2026, $440 million in second quarter and $1.467 billion in third quarter as Sandisk started shipping against long-term New Business Model contracts. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

This was the segment that made the standalone thesis intelligible to growth investors. The company did not need to persuade the market that consumer flash existed; it needed to show that datacenter storage could become large enough to reshape the earnings mix of a business still carrying the volatility of NAND pricing. The jump from $325 million of Cloud revenue in fiscal 2024 to a run-rate that produced $1.467 billion of Datacenter revenue in one quarter by April 2026 showed why the market's attention shifted.

Sandisk's January 2026 earnings release made the quality of that growth more explicit. Management said Datacenter demand was being driven by AI infrastructure builders, semi-custom customers and technology companies deploying AI at scale. By spring 2026, a single quarter of Datacenter revenue was already larger than the full-year Cloud revenue Sandisk had disclosed for fiscal 2024. [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## Client / Edge

Client was still the largest annual bucket at the time of the spin. In fiscal 2025 it generated $4.127 billion of revenue, modestly above the $4.069 billion reported in fiscal 2024. This category carried a wider set of exposures than a simple PC-storage label would suggest. Sandisk used it for client SSDs and embedded flash sold into PCs, mobile devices, automotive systems, gaming hardware and other OEM channels rather than as a pure PC-storage line. In fiscal 2026 quarterly reporting, the company relabelled much of this middle bucket as Edge, which produced $1.387 billion in first quarter, $1.678 billion in second quarter and $3.663 billion in third quarter. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

That relabelling mattered because mobile and automotive were genuine end markets but not separately reported revenue lines. They sat inside the larger Client or Edge bucket in the company's own disclosure, alongside PC, gaming and other embedded uses.

## Consumer

Consumer remained the part of the company most visibly associated with the legacy SanDisk brand. The 10-K described a portfolio of removable flash cards, universal serial bus flash drives and retail solid-state drives sold through retail and channel routes to market. Consumer revenue was $2.268 billion in fiscal 2025, essentially flat against $2.269 billion in fiscal 2024 after recovering from $1.949 billion in fiscal 2023. In the April 2026 quarter alone, Consumer still contributed $820 million of revenue even after Datacenter had become the market's central focus, underscoring that the retail franchise remained economically meaningful rather than merely symbolic. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The filings also made clear that the spin did not instantly erase Western Digital branding from the shelf. Sandisk said certain products would continue to be sold for a limited transitional period under the Western Digital, WD and other brands. That mattered because the consumer presence transferred to Sandisk was broader than a single red-and-white logo. It included a portfolio architecture assembled inside Western Digital and only gradually disentangled after separation. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Mix Shift Inside Fiscal 2026

The quarterly Datacenter, Edge and Consumer reporting used in fiscal 2026 gave a more current picture than the annual Cloud, Client and Consumer table alone. In first quarter, the split was $269 million Datacenter, $1.387 billion Edge and $652 million Consumer. In second quarter it was $440 million, $1.678 billion and $907 million. In third quarter it was $1.467 billion, $3.663 billion and $820 million. Edge still remained the largest quarterly bucket through April 2026, which was an important reminder that Sandisk had not become a pure datacenter company overnight. But Datacenter was growing quickly enough to change the corporate conversation from channel recovery to AI-linked storage exposure. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## Why the Segment Map Mattered

The segment map explained why Sandisk could look mature and newly inflected at the same time. It was not simply a consumer-flash brand trying to grow an enterprise adjunct. Nor was it already a datacenter company with consumer leftovers attached. It was a three-part portfolio whose annual revenue base still leaned heavily on Client and Consumer, even as the quarter-to-quarter momentum was being driven by Datacenter. That was why the company could look mature and cyclical in one table, and newly inflected in the next. The segments were not contradictory. They were the bridge between the old SanDisk and the new Sandisk.

chapters.title: Pre-spin Flash segment history and post-spin trajectory
chapters.body:
## From a Shared-Fab System to a Standalone Income Statement

Sandisk's standalone financial profile still began with the same manufacturing architecture that had defined the business inside Western Digital. The company did not own a fully captive NAND network. In its 2025 annual report, it said it held a 49.9 per cent ownership position in each Flash Ventures entity and acquired approximately one-half of the flash-based memory wafers those ventures produced. That distinction mattered because a great deal of Sandisk's economics flowed not from open-market wafer purchases but from a long-lived, shared-capital manufacturing system in Japan. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The consequence is that Sandisk's reported results always had two layers. One layer was the familiar market story of NAND prices, mix and demand. The other was the fab-economics story: how a near-equal but not literally 50.0 per cent interest in shared ventures translated into cost of goods, capital calls and capacity rights. The general dependence on Kioxia was obvious. What the disclosed stake clarified was that the economics were more exact, and more structurally constrained, than a flat 50/50 label implied.

## The Real Revenue Cycle

The most important numerical anchor was the revenue baseline. Sandisk's own historical disclosures showed revenue of $9.754 billion in 2022, $6.086 billion in fiscal 2023, $6.663 billion in fiscal 2024 and $7.355 billion in fiscal 2025. The downturn was therefore severe but not small in absolute dollars. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

| Fiscal year | Revenue | Gross margin |
|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $6.086bn | 7.1% |
| 2024 | $6.663bn | 16.1% |
| 2025 | $7.355bn | 30.1% |

Those margin figures mattered as much as the revenue line. The recovery into fiscal 2025 was not merely a matter of selling more bits. It was a pricing-and-mix recovery strong enough to lift gross margin from 7.1 per cent in fiscal 2023 to 30.1 per cent in fiscal 2025. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

On the disclosed numbers, the cycle looked larger and more industrial than a simple mid-single-digit revenue rebound would suggest. A business falling from nearly $10 billion to just above $6 billion and then climbing back to $7.355 billion looked like a major memory franchise enduring a brutal but recognisable correction. Investors price those stories differently.

## End-Market Recovery, Not Just Price Recovery

The annual report also gave a clearer answer to what, exactly, recovered. In fiscal 2025, Cloud revenue reached $960 million, up from $325 million in fiscal 2024, while Client revenue was $4.127 billion and Consumer revenue $2.268 billion. That mix showed two things at once. First, the recovery was not purely datacenter-led; the largest revenue pool was still Client. Second, the datacenter or cloud component had moved sharply enough to matter. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The filings also gave a clearer answer on the consumer business. Public disclosures did not frame it as a simple asset-or-distraction debate, but they did provide enough evidence to answer it more concretely. Consumer revenue was $2.268 billion in fiscal 2025, almost identical to the $2.269 billion recorded in fiscal 2024 and materially above the $1.949 billion posted in fiscal 2023. That meant the consumer franchise remained a large, cash-generating part of the company even as Cloud expanded fastest. The better conclusion was not that management had left the question unresolved. It was that the filings showed Sandisk trying to add a datacenter engine without surrendering a still-sizeable consumer annuity. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Spin and the Reset of Comparability

The separation itself became effective on February 21, 2025, with regular-way trading beginning on February 24. That chronology meant the first reported post-spin quarter was never going to give investors a clean start line. Sandisk entered public trading in the final stretch of fiscal third quarter 2025, then had to build a standalone disclosure record on the fly. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [listing press release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-celebrates-nasdaq-listing-after-completing-separation)

The early standalone numbers therefore mattered less as isolated quarters than as a sequence. Fiscal third quarter 2025 still showed the scars of the trough, including a $1.83 billion goodwill impairment charge. Fiscal fourth quarter 2025 was profitable on a non-GAAP basis and closed the year with $7.355 billion of revenue. Fiscal first through third quarter 2026 then showed the real inflection, as datacenter mix and the new contract model began to overwhelm the old spot-market framing. [Sandisk Q3 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## New Business Model Economics

The most consequential new financial disclosure inside the frozen window was not a classical price or unit figure. It was the contract backlog embedded in the New Business Model agreements. As of April 3, 2026, the Form 10-Q said the transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations was $41.6 billion, of which $41.2 billion had not yet been billed and $0.4 billion had been recorded as contract liabilities. About 15 per cent of those remaining performance obligations were expected to be recognised as revenue over the next twelve months. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

That disclosure changed the way Sandisk had to be analysed. NAND companies are usually valued against spot prices, supply discipline, cost-per-bit curves and inventory cycles. Sandisk was still exposed to all of those forces. But by spring 2026 it also had a disclosed long-dated revenue commitment structure large enough to warrant a second analytical lens. The market was no longer being asked to judge only whether NAND prices would rise. It was being asked whether customer-backed, financially committed supply agreements could make part of the cycle less violent.

## Guarantees, Liabilities and What Was Actually at Risk

The same filing also narrowed one of the broader market shorthand claims. Remaining Flash Ventures lease guarantees were disclosed at yen 158 billion, or $993 million, not at more than $11 billion. Total contract liabilities were $511 million. Those were still meaningful obligations, particularly for a company newly outside Western Digital's balance sheet. But they pointed to a much more specific liability structure than the looser readings that had circulated alongside the RPO figure. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

## The Central Financial Question

The central financial question by May 23, 2026 was therefore sharper than before. It was not merely whether a NAND cycle recovery was under way. It plainly was. The question was whether Sandisk could convert that recovery into a different kind of earnings stream: one built on a larger datacenter mix, a still-resilient consumer base, improved gross margins and contract-backed revenue visibility, all while remaining tied to a shared-fab model that required coordination with Kioxia at every major capital turn. The numbers now showed a company farther along that transition than much of the market shorthand had implied.

chapters.title: Post-spin quarters and NAND cycle commentary
chapters.body:
## The Cycle That Made the Spin

The arithmetic of Sandisk's independence began with a downturn. Historical combined disclosures showed revenue of $9.754 billion in 2022, collapsing to $6.086 billion in fiscal 2023 before recovering to $6.663 billion in fiscal 2024 and $7.355 billion in fiscal 2025. The crisis that sharpened the case for separation was therefore a very large flash business enduring a multi-billion-dollar contraction, not a smaller franchise merely wobbling around the mid-single-digit billions. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

For Goeckeler and his team, that downturn sharpened rather than blurred the case for independence. The flash business needed its own capital story, its own investor base and its own reporting cadence. But the market did not get a clean quarter-zero. The separation was effective on February 21, 2025 and regular-way trading began on February 24, 2025, in the final stretch of fiscal third quarter. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [listing press release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-celebrates-nasdaq-listing-after-completing-separation)

## Fiscal Third Quarter 2025: A Rough Debut, but a Useful Baseline

The first reported quarter under the new ticker was still scarred by the trough. Fiscal third-quarter 2025 revenue was $1.695 billion, down 10 per cent sequentially. The company recorded a GAAP loss of $1.93 billion, driven largely by a $1.83 billion goodwill impairment charge, while non-GAAP loss per share was $0.30. Cloud revenue was $197 million, Client $927 million and Consumer $571 million. [Sandisk Q3 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2025-financial-results)

The quarter nevertheless mattered as more than a bad print. Management used it to introduce the storyline that would dominate the next year: early BiCS8 ramp, supply discipline, and a conviction that price increases and mix improvement were beginning. In other words, the first standalone quarter still belonged to the old cycle, but management was already trying to define it as the last quarter before a structurally different one.

## Fiscal Fourth Quarter 2025: First Evidence of Stabilisation

Fiscal fourth-quarter 2025 was the first quarter that looked like a viable base for a standalone company rather than a trough clean-up exercise. Revenue was $1.901 billion, up 12 per cent sequentially and above guidance. GAAP loss narrowed to $23 million, while non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $0.29. For the full year, Sandisk reported $7.355 billion of revenue, confirming that the business had already recovered materially from the fiscal-2023 lows before the market got its first full year of standalone accounts. [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## Fiscal First Quarter 2026: Mix Shift Becomes Visible

Fiscal first-quarter 2026 was where the post-spin narrative became concrete. Revenue rose to $2.308 billion, up 21 per cent sequentially and 23 per cent year over year. Datacenter revenue was $269 million, Edge revenue $1.387 billion and Consumer revenue $652 million. The company reported GAAP net income of $112 million, non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of $1.22, operating cash flow of $488 million and adjusted free cash flow of $448 million. Cash ended the quarter at about $1.4 billion, and management said the company had reached a net-cash position ahead of schedule. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results)

This was also the quarter in which the product roadmap became commercially visible. Management said BiCS8 accounted for 15 per cent of total bits shipped and was expected to become the majority of bit production by the end of fiscal 2026. The release also said the company was engaged with five major hyperscale customers, had two hyperscalers in qualification, and expected a third hyperscaler and a top storage OEM in calendar 2026. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## Fiscal Second Quarter 2026: Operating Leverage Arrives

Fiscal second-quarter 2026 showed how fast a recovering NAND business could re-rate once pricing and mix improved together. Revenue rose to $3.025 billion. GAAP gross margin reached 50.9 per cent, up from 29.8 per cent in the prior quarter. GAAP operating income was $1.065 billion and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $6.20. Datacenter revenue rose to $440 million, up 64 per cent sequentially and 76 per cent year over year. [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The critical point was not just that the quarter was better. It was that the improvement was coming from exactly the places management had been pointing to: higher-value customers, better product mix and stronger pricing. By this stage, Sandisk was no longer arguing only that the trough had passed. It was arguing that the business model itself was becoming more durable.

## Fiscal Third Quarter 2026: The New Business Model Becomes Real

Fiscal third-quarter 2026 was the decisive quarter inside the frozen window. Revenue reached $5.950 billion, up 97 per cent sequentially and 251 per cent year over year. Datacenter revenue surged to $1.467 billion from $440 million in the prior quarter. GAAP gross margin rose to 78.4 per cent. GAAP net income was $3.615 billion, while non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $23.41. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The quarter also delivered the balance-sheet and backlog disclosures that changed the valuation debate. Management said it had ended the quarter with three signed New Business Model agreements and signed two additional agreements early in fiscal fourth quarter. The accompanying Form 10-Q said the transaction price allocated to remaining performance obligations was $41.6 billion, of which $41.2 billion had not yet been billed and $0.4 billion had been recorded as contract liabilities. About 15 per cent of those obligations were expected to be recognised as revenue over the next twelve months. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

The guidance ladder itself became part of the story. In August 2025, Sandisk guided fiscal first-quarter 2026 revenue to $2.10 billion to $2.20 billion and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share to $0.70 to $0.90. In November it guided the second quarter to $2.55 billion to $2.65 billion and $3.00 to $3.40. In January it guided the third quarter to $4.40 billion to $4.80 billion and $12.00 to $14.00. By April it was guiding the fourth quarter to $7.75 billion to $8.25 billion and $30.00 to $33.00. Those step-ups were so large that the market was no longer looking at a routine cyclical recovery; it was looking at a business whose contract structure and end-market mix were being reset in real time. [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## What the Sequence Said

The quarter-by-quarter sequence showed a larger flash franchise that spent 2025 stabilising, then used fiscal 2026 to change its mix decisively toward datacenter and contract-backed revenue.

That did not abolish the NAND cycle. It did, however, create a new interpretive frame. By the time the frozen window closed on May 23, 2026, Sandisk's earnings story was no longer just about recovering spot prices or disciplined underloading. It was about whether a historically volatile memory producer had finally found a way to lock part of its future demand into longer-duration economic commitments.

chapters.title: Goeckeler, CFO, and the post-spin board
chapters.body:
## The Executive Continuity Signal

The clearest governance signal in the separation was that David V. Goeckeler did not stay with the retained hard-disk-drive company. He crossed with the flash business and became chief executive of Sandisk. The final information statement said he had served as Western Digital's chief executive since March 2020 and had previously held senior leadership roles at Cisco Systems. In November 2024, before the spin closed, he was also elected chair of the Semiconductor Industry Association. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [SIA release](https://www.semiconductors.org/western-digital-ceo-david-goeckeler-elected-chair-of-semiconductor-industry-association/)

That continuity mattered more than the title alone suggested. Sandisk did not need a transition chief executive to explain the spin. It kept the executive who had already managed the 2023 trough, the strategic review and the internal reshaping of the flash business. In governance terms, the message was that the separation was not a prelude to a sale process or a caretaker phase. It was meant to be run.

## The Finance and Technology Layer

The filings were more specific about the CFO seat than a generic leadership sketch would have suggested. Sandisk's proxy statement said Luis F. Visoso had served as executive vice president and chief financial officer since February 2025. It also laid out a substantial operating background: immediately before the separation he had been Western Digital's executive vice president and chief administrative officer; before that he had served as chief financial officer at Unity Software and Palo Alto Networks and had held senior finance roles at Amazon Web Services, Cisco Systems and Procter & Gamble. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828025044481/sndk-20251006.htm)

That biography mattered because Sandisk's finance problem was not a simple controller's exercise. The company had to explain a capital-intensive shared-fab structure, a newly standalone balance sheet and an earnings profile being reshaped by long-duration customer commitments. Visoso was not just a reporting officer. He was one of the key translators of the new business model to the market.

The same proxy also filled in the technology leadership beneath the chief executive and finance roles. Alper Ilkbahar became executive vice president and chief technology officer in March 2025 after serving as senior vice president of global strategy and technology at Western Digital. Earlier in his career he had led the Intel Optane Group and had spent a decade at the prior SanDisk Corporation. That mattered because Sandisk's core strategic question by May 23, 2026 was not merely capital allocation. It was node transition and product execution. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828025044481/sndk-20251006.htm)

## The Board at Spin and the Board by May 2026

The spin-era nine-director board was not the same board investors were looking at by May 2026. The final information statement described the initial post-spin board. But at Sandisk's annual meeting on November 18, 2025, stockholders elected only seven directors: Richard B. Cassidy II, Thomas Caulfield, David V. Goeckeler, Devinder Kumar, Necip Sayiner, Ellyn J. Shook and Miyuki Suzuki. Then, effective December 30, 2025, Sandisk appointed Alexander R. Bradley to the board and to the audit committee. By May 23, 2026, the current board therefore comprised eight directors, not nine. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [2025 annual-meeting 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000119312525289885/d97202d8k.htm) [Bradley appointment release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-appoints-alexander-r-bradley-its-board-directors)

## The Current Board

| Director | Filing-backed description | Why it mattered |
|---|---|---|
| David V. Goeckeler | Chief executive officer of Sandisk; former Western Digital CEO | Separation continuity and operating accountability |
| Richard B. Cassidy II | Former chairman and CEO of TSMC Arizona; previously president and CEO of TSMC North America | Deep foundry and semiconductor manufacturing pattern recognition |
| Thomas Caulfield | Former CEO and later executive chair of GlobalFoundries | Capital allocation and large-scale semiconductor manufacturing governance |
| Devinder Kumar | Former CFO of AMD | Finance and audit depth from a cyclical semiconductor peer |
| Necip Sayiner | Former executive vice president and general manager at Renesas Electronics | Operating experience across semiconductor manufacturing and Japan-linked industry networks |
| Ellyn J. Shook | Former chief leadership and human resources officer at Accenture | Organisational build-out for a newly independent company |
| Miyuki Suzuki | Former president of Asia Pacific for Cisco Systems | Asia operating depth and regional commercial perspective |
| Alexander R. Bradley | CFO of First Solar at the time of appointment | Fresh public-company finance expertise added after the first annual meeting |

Sandisk's own proxy was narrower and more precise about Cassidy's background. It described him as former chairman and CEO of TSMC Arizona, and Sandisk's board biography also described him as former president and CEO of TSMC North America. That still made him one of the more relevant semiconductor manufacturing voices on the board, but the filing record did not describe him as having run Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. as a whole. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828025044481/sndk-20251006.htm) [Rick Cassidy board biography](https://investor.sandisk.com/board-member/rick-cassidy)

## A Board Built for Operations, Not Financial Engineering

Even after the correction, the broader observation still held. This was a board with an unusually heavy operating tilt for a mid-cap storage company. The proxy biographies leaned toward semiconductor executives, manufacturing operators, finance chiefs and organisational builders rather than dealmakers. Caulfield and Cassidy brought fab and foundry experience. Kumar brought chip-company finance. Sayiner brought another layer of semiconductor operating depth. Bradley's later addition strengthened the public-company finance bench even further. [2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828025044481/sndk-20251006.htm) [Bradley appointment release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-appoints-alexander-r-bradley-its-board-directors)

That mattered because Sandisk's live problems were operational. The company had to manage a shared Japanese manufacturing network, a technology transition portfolio that no longer fit the old shorthand of "BiCS 9 equals 300-plus layers," and a datacenter contract model that could reshape the earnings base if executed properly. It did not need a board built primarily to sell itself. It needed a board able to interrogate wafer economics, customer commitments and capital timing.

## The Real Governance Signal

By May 23, 2026, the governance signal was therefore not simply that Sandisk had recognisable names on its board. It was that the composition had already evolved after the spin. The initial nine-director slate gave way to a seven-director election at the first annual meeting, then an eight-member board with Bradley's addition. That sequence underscored that Sandisk was already behaving like an operating company settling into its own cadence rather than a freshly separated asset preserved in first-day form.

chapters.title: Consumer, enterprise SSD, OEMs, and the Kioxia JV manufacturing
chapters.body:
## A Customer Base That Ran from Retail to Hyperscalers

When Sandisk separated from Western Digital, it inherited a customer base that was broader than the usual memory-company caricature. The 2025 annual report said the company sold to computer manufacturers and OEMs, cloud service providers, resellers, distributors and retailers around the world. That mattered because Sandisk was not simply a hyperscaler supplier trying to preserve a legacy consumer business, nor merely a retail-flash brand attempting an enterprise pivot. It was both at once. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The concentration figures in the filing gave a more exact picture. For fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2024, no single customer accounted for more than 10 per cent of net revenue. In fiscal 2023, one customer accounted for 15 per cent. The top 10 customers accounted for 40 per cent of net revenue in fiscal 2025, 41 per cent in fiscal 2024 and 47 per cent in fiscal 2023. As of June 27, 2025, one customer represented about 11 per cent of accounts receivable. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

Those figures pointed to a business with meaningful concentration, but not one dependent on a single overwhelmingly dominant buyer by May 23, 2026. That was an important correction because the market's focus on hyperscaler demand could easily have obscured the continued breadth of Sandisk's channel exposure.

## Consumer Shelf Space, OEM Channels and the Datacenter Push

The consumer side of the franchise still rested on the SanDisk brand and the retail distribution muscle accumulated over decades in removable cards, USB drives and portable SSDs. At the same time, the annual report made clear that certain products would continue to be sold for a limited transitional period under the Western Digital, WD and other brands. The spin did not instantly collapse Sandisk's market presence into a single label. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The OEM and cloud channels were where the mix was changing fastest. In fiscal first-quarter 2026, management said it was engaged with five major hyperscale customers, had two hyperscalers in qualification and expected a third hyperscaler and a top storage OEM in calendar 2026. By fiscal third-quarter 2026, the company said it had ended the quarter with three signed New Business Model agreements and had signed two more early in the following quarter. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

That sequence showed a portfolio becoming more contract-heavy at the top end while still retaining the mass-market consumer and OEM breadth that had always characterised the brand. The datacenter story was new in scale. The channel diversity was not. The 10-K also said the company performed ongoing credit evaluations of customers' financial condition and generally required no collateral, a reminder that working-capital discipline still mattered even as the conversation shifted toward hyperscaler contracts.

The quarterly guidance ladder showed how quickly those top-end relationships were beginning to shape internal planning. Sandisk moved from guiding fiscal second-quarter 2026 revenue to $2.55 billion to $2.65 billion in November 2025, to guiding fiscal third-quarter revenue to $4.40 billion to $4.80 billion in January 2026, and then to guiding fiscal fourth-quarter revenue to $7.75 billion to $8.25 billion in April 2026. Management was plainly not planning around a generic retail rebound. It was planning around a much larger committed-demand ramp at the upper end of the portfolio. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Real Supply Chain: Flash Ventures First

The supply-side correction was even more important. The Kioxia relationship was often reduced to a flat 50/50 formula. Sandisk's 10-K was more precise. The company said it held a 49.9 per cent ownership position in each Flash Ventures entity and acquired approximately one-half of the flash-based memory wafers produced by those entities. The filing also said substantially all of Sandisk's flash memory wafers were supplied from Flash Ventures, while its controller wafers were all manufactured by third-party sources. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That meant Sandisk's supply chain had two different kinds of dependency. On the memory side, it was highly concentrated inside the Japanese joint-venture system. On the controller side, it depended entirely on external foundry and supply partners. The company therefore did not face one monolithic supply risk. It faced a layered one: a shared-capital memory network on one side and third-party semiconductor sourcing on the other.

## Yokkaichi, Kitakami and the 2034 Extension

The industrial footprint remained anchored in Japan. When Kioxia and Sandisk extended the Yokkaichi joint-venture agreements in January 2026, they also aligned the Kitakami agreements through December 31, 2034. Sandisk agreed to pay Kioxia $1.165 billion in instalments from 2026 through 2029 for manufacturing services and continued supply availability. [Kioxia-Sandisk Yokkaichi extension](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kioxia-and-sandisk-extend-yokkaichi-joint-venture-agreement)

That extension was not just a legal housekeeping item. It was a signal that both parties still preferred deeper industrial commitment to strategic ambiguity. By May 23, 2026, the relationship had survived Toshiba's corporate upheaval, Western Digital's acquisition of SanDisk, the aborted WDC-Kioxia transaction discussions of earlier years, and Sandisk's own re-spin. The supply chain was not being simplified. It was being reaffirmed.

## Geography, Assembly and Currency

The annual report also clarified that the company was not operationally confined to the Japanese fabs. It said Sandisk's operations outside the United States included owned manufacturing facilities in Malaysia, manufacturing operations contracted via related parties in China and Japan, and sales offices across the Americas, Asia Pacific, Europe and the Middle East. Those disclosures mattered because they showed how the wafer base in Japan flowed into a broader assembly, test and commercial network. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

They also explained why currency mattered. A business with large yen-linked manufacturing commitments and largely dollar-denominated end revenue carries embedded foreign-exchange exposure even before one gets to the customer mix or to reported segment margins. The filing-backed supply map made clear why that exposure was structurally unavoidable.

## What the Customer and Supply Map Implied

The picture was therefore more nuanced than simple bull-or-bear caricatures suggested. Sandisk was not narrowly concentrated on one buyer, but its top-10 customer base still accounted for 40 per cent of revenue. It was not simply a captive fab operator, but substantially all of its flash memory wafers still came from Flash Ventures. It was not merely a retailer's brand, but consumer remained large even as datacenter contracts became the market's focus.

That combination was the actual architecture of the company by May 23, 2026: broad commercial reach, increasingly important hyperscaler relationships, and a supply system whose resilience depended on the continued health of a single Japanese manufacturing partnership.

chapters.title: Where SanDisk sits against Samsung, Micron, Kioxia, Solidigm
chapters.body:
## Five Principal Rivals, and a Better Frame Than Point-in-Time Share Tables

The competitive picture was better framed through the company's own disclosures than through precise external market-share estimates. Sandisk's own annual report used a broader and more defensible framing. It said the company competed with vertically integrated suppliers such as Kioxia, Micron Technology, Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Yangtze Memory Technologies, as well as numerous smaller companies that assemble flash storage products. That list was the right starting point because it came from the company's own risk and competition disclosure rather than from a point-in-time external share estimate. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The critical competitive fact was not who held exactly 14 per cent or 22 per cent of global bits in any given quarter. It was that Sandisk operated inside a tightly concentrated NAND industry in which every serious rival either owned fabs outright, controlled adjacent memory franchises, or in Kioxia's case sat inside Sandisk's own manufacturing system.

## Samsung: Scale and Vertical Freedom

Samsung remained the benchmark competitor because it combined scale, a fully internal manufacturing chain and the financial capacity to endure margin compression that would be painful for a pure-play NAND issuer. Sandisk's filings repeatedly highlighted exposure to pricing competition and technology transitions; Samsung embodied both of those pressures. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The practical difference was not merely that Samsung was larger. It was that Samsung did not need a partner's consent to time a capacity addition or a technology transition. Sandisk's most important manufacturing decisions still had to fit inside the logic of Flash Ventures. Samsung's did not. That left Sandisk with less unilateral flexibility in downturns and less unilateral speed in recoveries, even if the Kioxia partnership partially compensated through shared scale.

## Micron: The Closest US Memory Peer

Micron was the closest US-based memory peer, but it represented a different strategic model. Micron combined NAND with DRAM and retained a stronger domestic-policy angle inside US semiconductor discussions. Sandisk, by contrast, was a pure-play NAND company whose core manufacturing base remained in Japan through the Kioxia partnership. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That made the comparison instructive. Micron and Sandisk both needed to keep up on cost-per-bit and enterprise product performance. But Micron's corporate diversification across memory types and Sandisk's tighter single-franchise focus meant investors were not really being offered the same risk package. Sandisk's competitive pitch was sharper focus. Micron's was broader memory-system exposure.

## SK Hynix and the Solidigm Axis

SK Hynix mattered not only as a large memory manufacturer but also through the enterprise SSD capabilities it had assembled from Intel's former NAND business. That axis was important because Sandisk's own strategic re-rating depended heavily on datacenter SSD growth. The company itself underscored the importance of SK Hynix enough that, in August 2025, it announced a collaboration with SK Hynix to help standardise High Bandwidth Flash technology for AI inference workloads. Rivals do not usually cooperate unless both acknowledge the strategic importance of the category. [Sandisk SK Hynix HBF release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-collaborate-sk-hynix-drive-standardization-high)

The better way to read SK Hynix in Sandisk's competitive map, therefore, was not through a narrow product-comparison table. It was as a rival strong enough in memory and enterprise storage to force Sandisk simultaneously to compete and, in one future-facing technology segment, to collaborate.

## Kioxia: Partner and Competitor in the Same Breath

Kioxia remained the most structurally unusual rival because it sat both inside and outside Sandisk's economic perimeter. The 10-K said Sandisk held 49.9 per cent ownership positions in the Flash Ventures entities and acquired approximately one-half of the wafers produced there. That meant Kioxia was inseparable from Sandisk's cost base. It also meant Kioxia was inseparable from Sandisk's competitive exposure, because both companies then sold finished products built on related NAND technology into overlapping end markets. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

This partner-rival structure was why simplistic share tables obscured more than they clarified. Sandisk was not just one more standalone vendor chasing wafers in the open market. It was a company whose primary manufacturing ally also had its own public shareholders, product ambitions and incentives. That was a strategic complication none of Samsung, Micron or SK Hynix had to manage in quite the same way.

## YMTC and the Lower-End Pricing Threat

Yangtze Memory Technologies belonged in the competitive set because Sandisk itself named it in the 10-K. The significance was less about near-term parity in the highest-end enterprise products and more about the persistent pricing pressure a state-backed Chinese NAND competitor could exert across parts of the flash value chain, especially in categories closer to the consumer end of the market. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That mattered because Sandisk still derived more than $2.2 billion of annual revenue from Consumer in fiscal 2025. A company that wanted to be re-rated on datacenter growth still needed to protect the margins of its consumer franchise. YMTC was one of the reasons that was difficult.

## Where Sandisk Actually Differentiated

Sandisk's differentiation claim looked cleaner when framed through the company's own disclosures. It rested on three things.

First, the company had a globally recognised consumer franchise that still produced meaningful revenue and channel presence. Second, it had access to a very large manufacturing system through Flash Ventures without bearing the full burden of a wholly captive fab network. Third, by fiscal 2026 it had begun to prove that datacenter demand could become large enough to reshape the corporate mix, with Datacenter revenue moving from $269 million in fiscal first-quarter 2026 to $1.467 billion in fiscal third-quarter 2026. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

Those were real advantages, but they were incomplete ones. The consumer brand did not solve the problem of shared manufacturing governance. The joint venture did not solve the problem of competing against fully integrated giants. And the datacenter ramp, while dramatic, was still new enough by May 23, 2026 to require proof that the contract-backed demand was durable.

## The Competitive Reality at the Snapshot Date

The competitive picture was therefore less flashy and more credible than a synthetic share table suggested. Sandisk did not need a fabricated market-share table to look strategically relevant. It already occupied a rare position: a pure-play NAND company with a large consumer business, a meaningful datacenter ramp, and a manufacturing partnership that was simultaneously its moat and one of its greatest constraints. That combination was exactly why the stock was interesting, and exactly why the competition remained so unforgiving.

chapters.title: From 2016 WDC acquisition through 2025 spin and BiCS 8 ramp
chapters.body:
## The Separation Itself

The single most important catalyst was the one that created the company in its present form. Western Digital completed the separation of its Flash business on February 21, 2025, and Sandisk said regular-way trading began on Nasdaq on February 24. That legal and trading chronology was the starting point for everything that followed: a business that had been buried inside a mixed HDD-and-flash reporting structure now had its own ticker, its own board and its own capital story. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [listing press release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-celebrates-nasdaq-listing-after-completing-separation)

## The First Operating Reset

The first operating catalysts were the two quarters that established whether Sandisk could emerge from the spin as more than a structural curiosity. Fiscal third-quarter 2025 revenue was $1.695 billion, still weighed down by a $1.83 billion goodwill impairment charge and a non-GAAP loss per share of $0.30. Fiscal fourth-quarter 2025 revenue then improved to $1.901 billion, above guidance, while non-GAAP diluted earnings per share turned positive at $0.29 and full-year revenue reached $7.355 billion. Those disclosures mattered because they gave investors both a trough print and a first stabilisation print within six months of the spin. [Sandisk Q3 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results)

## The Guidance Stair-Step

One of the clearest catalysts through the frozen window was not a single event but the speed at which management kept resetting its own expectations upward. In August 2025, Sandisk guided fiscal first-quarter 2026 revenue to $2.10 billion to $2.20 billion and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share to $0.70 to $0.90. In November, after delivering $2.308 billion of first-quarter revenue, it guided the second quarter to $2.55 billion to $2.65 billion and $3.00 to $3.40 of non-GAAP EPS. In January 2026 it guided the third quarter to $4.40 billion to $4.80 billion and $12.00 to $14.00. In April it guided the fourth quarter to $7.75 billion to $8.25 billion and $30.00 to $33.00. That staircase of guidance increases was itself a catalyst because it forced investors to re-underwrite the earnings power of the business quarter after quarter. [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## The Technology and Standards Signals

The second catalyst cluster was technological, but more nuanced than a single-node story. On February 20, 2025, one trading day before the legal separation, Kioxia and Sandisk previewed 10th-generation 3D flash memory with 332 world-lines and a 59 per cent improvement in bit density. Later, on November 7, 2025, Kioxia said 9th-generation BiCS FLASH 512Gb TLC devices had entered sampling on a 120-layer process using CBA technology. Those disclosures mattered because they turned the roadmap into a sequence of concrete milestones rather than a vague assertion about future layer counts. [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices)

Sandisk added a more speculative but still important technology signal in August 2025 when it announced a collaboration with SK Hynix to help standardise High Bandwidth Flash for AI inference workloads. Sandisk said the work was enabled by its BiCS technology and proprietary CBA wafer bonding, targeted first HBF samples in the second half of calendar 2026, and expected the first AI-inference devices with HBF in early 2027. That was not yet a shipping revenue stream by May 23, 2026. It was a catalyst because it widened the range of markets in which Sandisk was trying to be relevant to AI infrastructure. [Sandisk SK Hynix HBF release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-collaborate-sk-hynix-drive-standardization-high)

## The Manufacturing Overhang Lifts

Another major catalyst arrived on January 29, 2026, when Kioxia and Sandisk extended the Yokkaichi joint-venture agreements through December 31, 2034 and aligned the Kitakami arrangements to the same end date. Sandisk agreed to pay Kioxia $1.165 billion over 2026 to 2029 for manufacturing services and continued supply availability. The extension removed an obvious strategic overhang, because a company whose cost base depended on Japanese joint ventures could not have afforded lingering uncertainty over the term of those agreements just as its datacenter business was accelerating. [Kioxia-Sandisk Yokkaichi extension](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kioxia-and-sandisk-extend-yokkaichi-joint-venture-agreement)

## The Datacenter and NBM Inflection

The final and most powerful catalyst through May 23, 2026 was the new contract model layered on top of the datacenter ramp. Fiscal first-quarter 2026 revenue was $2.308 billion, including $269 million of Datacenter revenue. Fiscal second quarter rose to $3.025 billion, with Datacenter at $440 million. Fiscal third quarter then jumped to $5.950 billion, with Datacenter at $1.467 billion. Management said it ended the third quarter with three signed New Business Model agreements and signed two more early in fiscal fourth quarter. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

The accompanying Form 10-Q supplied the hard metric that turned that narrative into a balance-sheet issue. As of April 3, 2026, Sandisk disclosed $41.6 billion of remaining performance obligations, with $41.2 billion unbilled and about 15 per cent expected to be recognised as revenue over the next twelve months. That was the moment the market stopped asking only whether NAND pricing was recovering and started asking whether Sandisk was building a different economic model on top of the recovery. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

## What the Market Actually Needed to See

By the end of the frozen window, the catalysts were easier to rank than they had been at the spin. Separation created the investable object. Stabilisation quarters made it credible. The guidance ladder forced repeated upward revisions. The Yokkaichi extension de-risked the manufacturing foundation. And the NBM disclosures gave investors a framework for believing that Sandisk might be becoming something more than a cleanly timed NAND-cycle trade. The answer was still unfinished by May 23, 2026, but the primary-source record already showed why the stock had become a much more consequential story than a routine spin-off.

chapters.title: BiCS NAND technology, Kioxia JV development, broader patents
chapters.body:
## The IP Estate the Spin Carried Across

Sandisk's intellectual property mattered, and the public filings made that importance more concrete than a generic patent reference would have. In the 2025 annual report, the company said it had approximately 7,900 granted patents and approximately 3,200 pending patent applications worldwide. It described those patents as one of the attributes underpinning its position in the Consumer end market and in flash more broadly. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That disclosure changed the tone of the chapter. Sandisk was not merely a company with some legacy NAND patents lingering from the Harari era. It was a large, still-active IP holder whose estate spanned device architecture, controllers, systems integration and manufacturing know-how accumulated across the Western Digital years and the older SanDisk lineage.

## BiCS8 Was the Production Fact Pattern

The annual report and quarterly releases supported one point clearly: BiCS8 was the production node that mattered in the early standalone period. Sandisk's quarterly results said BiCS8 accounted for 15 per cent of bits shipped in fiscal first-quarter 2026 and was expected to become the majority of bit production by the end of fiscal 2026. That was the filing-backed fact pattern for the node that carried the company into its public-market reintroduction. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results)

BiCS8 itself was straightforward. What required more care was the rest of the roadmap, because the public disclosures did not present it as a simple linear staircase. The relevant primary-source roadmap inside the frozen window came from two later disclosures.

## What the Companies Actually Said About the Next Nodes

First, on February 20, 2025, Kioxia and Sandisk previewed 10th-generation 3D flash memory technology with 332 world-lines and a 59 per cent improvement in bit density, as well as faster interface speed and reduced power consumption. Second, on November 7, 2025, Kioxia said 9th-generation BiCS FLASH 512Gb TLC devices had entered sampling on a 120-layer process using CBA technology, with mass production planned for fiscal 2025. [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices)

Those disclosures did not fit a simple shorthand of "BiCS 9 equals 300-plus layers." They showed a public roadmap that combined an in-market BiCS8 ramp, a sampled 9th-generation part on a 120-layer process and a more aggressive 10th-generation preview at 332 world-lines. This was not a cosmetic distinction. It changed how one thought about execution risk. Sandisk and Kioxia were no longer being judged only on adding layers to a single known node.
