They were juggling a more complex transition path involving CBA process choices, density gains and future interface performance.

## R&D Beyond the Core NAND Node

The public record through May 23, 2026 also showed that Sandisk's R&D agenda was beginning to extend beyond conventional NAND bit-density marketing. In August 2025, the company said it had signed a memorandum of understanding with SK Hynix to help establish the specification for High Bandwidth Flash, a technology it positioned for next-generation AI inference workloads. Sandisk said it targeted first HBF samples in the second half of calendar 2026 and expected the first AI-inference devices using HBF in early 2027. [Sandisk SK Hynix HBF release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-collaborate-sk-hynix-drive-standardization-high)

That announcement mattered for two reasons. First, it showed Sandisk trying to shape standards rather than merely follow them. Second, it suggested that the company wanted an answer to the question hanging over the whole memory stack in the AI era: whether flash could move closer to high-bandwidth, higher-value inference workloads rather than remaining a lower-multiple storage substrate behind the accelerator story.

## Licensing Revenue Was Acknowledged but Not Broken Out

Public filings also allowed a more precise answer on licensing revenue. Sandisk's 2025 annual report said license and royalty revenue was attributed geographically based on the headquarters location of the licensee, which confirmed that such revenue existed. But the company did not separately disclose a standalone licensing-revenue line in the annual report. The April 2026 Form 10-Q added that the company used the disclosure practical expedient for sale-based or usage-based royalties for intellectual property license arrangements, which typically run longer than one year. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

That meant the correct statement was not simply that public disclosures "did not separately break out" the income. The fuller, researched version was that Sandisk explicitly acknowledged license and royalty revenue in its geographic revenue note and in its revenue-recognition disclosure, but still did not quantify it as its own reported line item. Licensing therefore remained economically real and analytically relevant, yet not cleanly isolatable from the public filings alone.

## Why the IP Story Mattered Financially

The reason the IP story mattered financially was not just that patent counts were large. It was that Sandisk's differentiation claim sat partly in technology and partly in economic rights. The company was trying to prove that it could use jointly developed NAND technology, a large patent estate and future-oriented projects such as HBF to escape being valued as nothing more than a leveraged play on commodity flash pricing.

That proposition was not fully proven by May 23, 2026. But the primary-source record was still stronger than a generic technology summary would have suggested. Sandisk had a very large active patent portfolio, a live and evolving node roadmap, and enough publicly disclosed licensing activity to show that its IP sat inside the business model rather than beside it as a historical relic.

chapters.title: NAND cycle, Kioxia JV economics, competitive intensity, post-spin execution
chapters.body:
The risk profile confronting Sandisk at the moment of its independence was still defined by cyclical memory economics, but the primary-source record clarified the scale and shape of that risk. The company was not emerging from a small flash business with a vaguely described fab arrangement. It was emerging from a $7.355 billion fiscal-2025 revenue base tied to a 49.9 per cent economic interest in a shared Japanese manufacturing system and a datacenter ramp that was already large enough to matter. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## NAND Cycle Volatility

The first risk remained the oldest one: NAND pricing volatility. Historical combined disclosures showed revenue at $9.754 billion in 2022, $6.086 billion in fiscal 2023, $6.663 billion in fiscal 2024 and $7.355 billion in fiscal 2025. Gross margin fell to 7.1 per cent in fiscal 2023 before recovering to 30.1 per cent in fiscal 2025. That was the real amplitude of the cycle Sandisk had to survive as a standalone public company. [final information statement](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/aa2fb019-6782-45f8-a9ff-108486c78c0a) [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

The point was not simply that revenue could swing. It was that margins could compress to levels that left little room for strategic error. A company that posted 7.1 per cent gross margin in one fiscal year and 30.1 per cent two years later was still, by definition, exposed to a violent commodity cycle even if its product mix was improving.

## Flash Ventures Concentration

The second risk sat in the manufacturing model. Sandisk said it held 49.9 per cent ownership positions in the Flash Ventures entities and acquired approximately one-half of the flash-based memory wafers they produced. It also said substantially all of its flash memory wafers were supplied from Flash Ventures, while controller wafers were all manufactured by third-party sources. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

That meant the company faced concentration on two fronts at once: dependence on the Kioxia-linked venture system for memory wafers and dependence on outside suppliers for controllers. The existence of dependency was obvious. The filings showed how close to total it actually was on the flash-memory side.

## Customer Concentration and Mix Risk

The third risk was commercial concentration. No single customer represented more than 10 per cent of net revenue in fiscal 2025 or fiscal 2024, but one customer had represented 15 per cent in fiscal 2023, and the top 10 customers still accounted for 40 per cent of revenue in fiscal 2025. One customer also represented about 11 per cent of accounts receivable as of June 27, 2025. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

This mattered especially because the corporate narrative was shifting toward datacenter and hyperscalers at the same time. In fiscal first-quarter 2026, management said it was engaged with five major hyperscale customers. By fiscal third-quarter 2026, the NBM contract model had become central to the earnings story. Greater visibility can improve quality of revenue. It can also increase dependence on a smaller group of very large buyers. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## Technology-Transition Risk

The fourth risk was that the public roadmap was more complex than a simple outside description suggested. BiCS8 was the current production node, but the official forward-looking disclosures inside the frozen window included a February 2025 preview of 10th-generation 3D flash memory with 332 world-lines and a November 2025 announcement that 9th-generation 512Gb TLC devices had entered sampling on a 120-layer process using CBA technology. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices)

That did not mean the roadmap was broken. It meant outsiders had less clean visibility into the sequence than a simple "BiCS9 at 300-plus layers" formulation implied. For investors, that increased execution risk. A company is easier to underwrite when the node path is simple, incremental and well quantified. Sandisk's published path was more ambitious and more layered than that.

## Competitive Intensity

The fifth risk was competitive intensity from the group Sandisk itself named: Kioxia, Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix, Yangtze Memory Technologies and smaller flash assemblers. This was not a market in which a mis-timed product transition could be hidden. Every delay, every cost miss and every pricing concession showed up against competitors that either owned their own fabs outright or carried different forms of state backing, memory diversification or scale. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

Kioxia was the most complicated risk because it was also the closest manufacturing partner. Samsung was the scale risk. Micron was the US memory-peer risk. SK Hynix was the enterprise-storage and technology-standardisation risk. YMTC was the lower-end pricing pressure risk. Sandisk did not face one rival. It faced a set of structurally different rivals at the same time.

## New Business Model Execution Risk

The sixth risk was the one the market had begun to celebrate: the New Business Model itself. The April 2026 Form 10-Q disclosed $41.6 billion of remaining performance obligations, with $41.2 billion unbilled and $0.4 billion recorded as contract liabilities. It also disclosed total contract liabilities of $511 million and remaining Flash Ventures lease guarantees of yen 158 billion, or $993 million. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

Those numbers were more precise than casual shorthand implied, but they still created a new class of risk. If the NBM agreements performed as intended, they could make revenue more visible and margins more durable. If qualification, volume ramp, customer behaviour or supply execution fell short, the same contracts could create operational strain, contractual disputes or investor disappointment precisely because expectations had moved so far, so fast.

## Foreign-Exchange and Geopolitical Exposure

The seventh risk remained geographic. The company disclosed owned manufacturing facilities in Malaysia, manufacturing operations contracted via related parties in China and Japan, and a core NAND-production base tied to Japan through Flash Ventures. That meant exposure to yen movements, trade-policy shifts and regional supply disruption was structural rather than incidental. [Sandisk 2025 10-K](https://investor.sandisk.com/static-files/342a38e2-e204-4f50-ad22-3e3a28e2f6ff)

## The Real Risk Frame

The risk frame was therefore harsher and more coherent at the same time. Sandisk had more revenue scale, better datacenter momentum and a more exact contract backlog than many quick reads of the story had assumed. But it also remained deeply exposed to cycle volatility, customer concentration, technology execution and a manufacturing structure whose strengths and constraints were inseparable. Those were the risks that mattered by May 23, 2026.

chapters.title: BiCS 9 ramp, AI data centre SSD, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Near-Term Outlook Was No Longer Just a Node Story

The near-term outlook could not be reduced to a single claim that BiCS9 would reach volume in 2026. Primary sources did not support that statement in that form. The better way to frame the outlook by May 23, 2026 was to separate three questions: how quickly BiCS8 would become the dominant production node, how the next-generation roadmap would move from public preview and sampling into high-volume production, and how much of Sandisk's improving earnings base was now tied to long-duration customer commitments rather than spot NAND pricing. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices)

## BiCS8 First, Then the Roadmap Beyond It

The only clearly disclosed production milestone was that BiCS8 accounted for 15 per cent of bits shipped in fiscal first-quarter 2026 and was expected to become the majority of bit production by the end of fiscal 2026. That was the filing-backed near-term node outlook. Beyond that, the public roadmap pointed to a November 2025 sampling milestone for 9th-generation 512Gb TLC devices and to a February 2025 preview of 10th-generation 332-world-line technology. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Kioxia 9th-generation BiCS sampling](https://blog-us.kioxia.com/post/2025/11/07/kioxia-begins-sampling-9th-generation-bics-flash-512-gb-tlc-devices) [Kioxia and Sandisk next-generation 3D flash preview](https://europe.kioxia.com/en-europe/business/news/2025/20250220-1.html)

That outlook was not weak. It was simply more conditional than a single-node narrative implied. The next phase depended on execution across multiple disclosed tracks rather than on one supposedly pre-announced mass-production date.

## Datacenter Had Become the Earnings Driver

The second leg of the outlook was commercial rather than technological. Datacenter revenue rose from $269 million in fiscal first-quarter 2026 to $440 million in fiscal second quarter and then to $1.467 billion in fiscal third quarter. At the same time, total revenue rose from $2.308 billion to $3.025 billion and then to $5.950 billion. The company's own quarterly disclosures therefore made clear that the near-term outlook rested heavily on whether the datacenter mix shift could continue. [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

This was also the clearest reason the company had begun to look less like a pure spot-market NAND trade. By April 2026, management was no longer speaking only about better demand and higher pricing. It was talking about a deliberate shift toward higher-value end markets backed by firm financial commitments. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## The Backlog and Balance-Sheet Questions

The third leg of the outlook sat in the new contract structure. As of April 3, 2026, the Form 10-Q disclosed $41.6 billion of remaining performance obligations, with about 15 per cent expected to convert into revenue over the next twelve months. The same quarter-end disclosure showed remaining Flash Ventures lease guarantees of yen 158 billion, or $993 million. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 Form 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2023554/000162828026029401/sndk-20260403.htm)

Those figures meant the medium-term outlook could no longer be read only through industry spot prices. A growing portion of the argument had to be made through contract conversion, customer retention and the operational discipline required to serve very large committed volumes. That was a potentially better business model. It was also a different kind of execution burden.

The speed with which management kept raising its own targets also shaped the outlook. After guiding fiscal first-quarter 2026 revenue to $2.10 billion to $2.20 billion in August 2025, Sandisk moved to $2.55 billion to $2.65 billion for the second quarter in November, $4.40 billion to $4.80 billion for the third quarter in January, and $7.75 billion to $8.25 billion for the fourth quarter in April. The guidance path itself suggested that management believed committed customer demand was becoming a more important variable than ordinary spot-market seasonality. [Sandisk Q4 FY25 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) [Sandisk Q1 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-first-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q2 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-second-quarter-2026-financial-results) [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## Guidance as of May 23, 2026

Sandisk's own near-term guidance at the end of the frozen window was aggressive. In the April 30, 2026 third-quarter release, the company said it expected fiscal fourth-quarter 2026 revenue of $7.75 billion to $8.25 billion and non-GAAP diluted earnings per share of $30.00 to $33.00. That guidance was still forward-looking and therefore contingent as of May 23, 2026, but it showed how dramatically management believed the earnings base had shifted. In the same release, Goeckeler said the company had a zero-debt balance sheet, strong cash generation and a recently authorised share-repurchase programme, underscoring how much the financial posture had changed from the trough conditions of 2023. [Sandisk Q3 FY26 release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-reports-fiscal-third-quarter-2026-financial-results)

## The Longer-Dated Technology Optionality

Beyond the near-term NAND cycle, the public record through May 23, 2026 also showed a more speculative but still relevant option in High Bandwidth Flash. In August 2025, Sandisk said it was working with SK Hynix on an HBF specification for AI inference workloads and was targeting first samples in the second half of calendar 2026, with the first AI-inference devices expected in early 2027. As of May 23, 2026, that was still an aspiration rather than a shipped business. But it showed management trying to broaden Sandisk's relevance to AI beyond conventional SSD supply. [Sandisk SK Hynix HBF release](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/sandisk-collaborate-sk-hynix-drive-standardization-high)

## The Real 2026-2030 Debate

The medium-term debate therefore rested on four linked propositions. First, that BiCS8 would become the dominant production node on schedule while the next-generation roadmap advanced from preview and sampling into scalable output. Second, that datacenter demand would stay large enough to keep mix moving away from lower-value bits. Third, that NBM agreements would convert backlog into durable economics rather than merely into one-off headline numbers. Fourth, that the Kioxia partnership, freshly extended through 2034, would keep giving Sandisk enough manufacturing scale to compete without trapping it in strategic paralysis. [Kioxia-Sandisk Yokkaichi extension](https://investor.sandisk.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kioxia-and-sandisk-extend-yokkaichi-joint-venture-agreement)

That was a more grounded outlook. It did not rely on a single unsupported production-date assertion. It relied on the disclosures available as of May 23, 2026, and those disclosures already showed a company whose future depended as much on commercial model execution as on the next layer count announced by its manufacturing partner.

financials.key_finding: SanDisk completed its spin-off from Western Digital February 21 2025 as a standalone NAND flash and SSD pure-play. Pre-spin Western Digital Flash segment FY2024 revenue was approximately $5B; post-spin SanDisk standalone first full fiscal year will reflect the NAND cycle dynamics plus the Kioxia JV economics plus the enterprise SSD AI data centre opportunity.
structural_observations: Kioxia JV with Japanese partner for NAND production at Yokkaichi and Kitakami fabs is principal manufacturing arrangement; JV economics are complex (50/50 capex share, output share).
BiCS 8 (218-layer) 3D NAND in volume production through 2025; BiCS 9 (300+ layer) in development.
Enterprise SSD market scaling on AI data centre storage demand; SanDisk competes with Samsung, Micron, Solidigm (SK Hynix), Kioxia.
Consumer NAND (microSD cards, USB drives, broader) SanDisk brand legacy.
CEO David Goeckeler continued from Western Digital where he was CEO 2020-February 2025.

leadership.key_finding: Sandisk's nine-director post-spin board pairs CEO David Goeckeler (current SIA Chairman; the executive who ran Western Digital through the EMC-era integration and the 2024-2025 strategic separation that spun Sandisk out) with an unusually deep semiconductor-CEO peer set: Richard B. Cassidy II (former TSMC Chairman/CEO), Thomas Caulfield (former GlobalFoundries CEO), Devinder Kumar (former AMD CFO), Necip Sayiner (former Renesas EVP). Plus Ellyn Shook (Accenture CLO/CHRO) and Miyuki Suzuki (Cisco Asia Pacific President). The composition is calibrated for operating governance of a pure-play NAND company through the BiCS8 ramp and the AI storage demand cycle, with the foundry-and-fab-CEO depth (Cassidy TSMC + Caulfield GlobalFoundries) being the most consequential single board characteristic.

ceo.name: David V. Goeckeler
ceo.title: Chief Executive Officer and Director (Class III)
ceo.external_role: Chair of the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) Board of Directors (elected November 2024)
ceo.framing: Goeckeler joined Western Digital as CEO in 2020 from Cisco where he was Executive Vice President and General Manager of the Networking and Security Business. He led WDC through the multi-year strategic review that culminated in the February 2025 separation of the Flash business into Sandisk Corporation. As SIA Chairman he is the senior US industry voice on semiconductor policy. His continuity as CEO of the spun-off Sandisk entity is the single most important governance signal of post-spin operating intent.

board_of_directors.name: Richard B. Cassidy II
board_of_directors.career: Former Chairman and CEO of TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company); brings the deepest foundry pedigree available on any US semiconductor board
board_of_directors.framing: The TSMC Chair/CEO credential is the most consequential single semiconductor industry leadership credential globally. Direct relevance to Sandisk's NAND fab strategy and BiCS8 capex execution.

board_of_directors.name: Thomas Caulfield
board_of_directors.career: Former CEO of GlobalFoundries Inc.; ran GF through its 2018 strategic refocus on mature nodes and 2021 NASDAQ IPO
board_of_directors.framing: GlobalFoundries CEO credential parallel to TSMC; provides US foundry pattern recognition with focus on capital allocation and process technology investment.

board_of_directors.name: Devinder Kumar
board_of_directors.career: Former Chief Financial Officer of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD); long-tenured AMD finance executive through the company's restructuring and AI accelerator cycle
board_of_directors.framing: AMD CFO credential through the Lisa Su era is the deepest single chip-company finance pedigree on the board. Critical for the Audit Committee oversight of a capex-intensive NAND business.

board_of_directors.name: Necip Sayiner
board_of_directors.career: Former Executive Vice President at Renesas Electronics; semiconductor industry operating executive
board_of_directors.framing: Renesas EVP brings Japanese-affiliated semiconductor industry operating depth — relevant to Sandisk's Kioxia joint venture relationship (legacy NAND fab partnership inherited from the Toshiba era).

board_of_directors.name: Ellyn J. Shook
board_of_directors.career: Former Chief Leadership and Human Resources Officer at Accenture; senior HR executive through Accenture's scale-up
board_of_directors.framing: Accenture CLO/CHRO credential brings global-scale leadership-development governance. Particularly relevant for a recently-spun-off public company building its independent corporate culture.

board_of_directors.name: Miyuki Suzuki
board_of_directors.career: Former President of Asia Pacific for Cisco Systems; Asia-region technology operating executive
board_of_directors.framing: Cisco Asia Pacific leadership credential complements Goeckeler's Cisco history; Asia regional operating depth maps to Sandisk's Asia manufacturing footprint.

leadership.board_composition_observation: The Sandisk post-spin board is unusually heavy on semiconductor-CEO peer credentials: TSMC (Cassidy), GlobalFoundries (Caulfield), AMD CFO (Kumar), and Renesas EVP (Sayiner). This concentration of senior chip-industry operating pedigree is rare for a sub-$15B market cap semiconductor company and reflects the strategic importance of the Sandisk separation to the broader US NAND industry. There is no separate independent investment-banking or financial-engineering director — the board is calibrated for operating governance of the BiCS8 ramp and the NAND pricing cycle, not for transactional M&A.

counterparties.key_finding: Sandisk's counterparty map is dominated by (a) hyperscaler / cloud data center customers buying enterprise SSDs (Datacenter segment $269M Q1 FY26), (b) consumer device OEMs and channel partners across mobile, PC, gaming consoles for the Edge and Consumer segments, (c) the Kioxia (formerly Toshiba) joint venture relationship — Sandisk's primary NAND fab partner inherited from the Western Digital era operating fabs in Yokkaichi and Kitakami, Japan, (d) the broader memory supply ecosystem (Samsung, SK Hynix, Micron, YMTC as competitors at the NAND industry level).

Consumer (retail SSDs, removable storage, gaming console NAND)

Kioxia is itself a publicly listed Japanese company (8035 Tokyo) as of 2024 IPO. The JV economics shape Sandisk's bit-output capacity and capex schedule.
